transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, Dr. [Your Name]. Well, honestly, I'm here because of this whole flying thing. It’s just... it's started to feel way, way scarier than it should. Like, I know logically that people fly safely every single day. I work at a daycare center, and we teach the kids about airplanes and how they go up in the sky, and it's all very normal. But for me, lately, just the idea of getting on a plane... it immediately makes me picture this one specific flight. My husband and I went on our honeymoon to Hawaii, which was supposed to be this amazing, relaxing trip, and the flight there was just... there was this horrible turbulence. Like, the kind where the plane drops and your stomach just stays up in your chest, and the flight attendants had to sit down quickly. I mean, we made it, obviously, but ever since then, I just can't shake that feeling. I start picturing the cabin shaking and the overhead bins rattling, and I just... I can't do it. And I know it's silly, I really do, because statistically, driving is so much more dangerous, and I drive to work every day without a second thought. But getting on a plane? It just feels impossible right now.

So your fear seems to be strongly connected to the turbulence you experienced on your flight to Hawaii. Is it mainly the idea of turbulence that scares you, or is it the whole experience of being on a plane that feels overwhelming now?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because I've spent so much time trying to figure that out myself. I mean, the turbulence is definitely the big thing, the main thing that flashes in my head when I think about it. I can still feel that drop, you know? But... it's kind of bled into everything else about flying now. It's not just the turbulence anymore. 

Like, even just thinking about the airport... the smell of the terminal, the way the boarding pass looks, standing in that little jet bridge thing before you get on the plane. It all just starts this... this reaction in me. It's like my brain knows that all those things lead to being trapped in that metal tube where the turbulence happens. And I know the pilots are trained, I know the planes are built to handle it, I've watched all these YouTube videos trying to educate myself on how aerodynamics work and how turbulence is just like bumps on a road, but it doesn't help. 

So I guess, to answer your question, it started with the turbulence, but now it's just the whole entire thing. Just the thought of booking a ticket makes my hands sweat. My husband was talking about going to visit his parents in Florida for Thanksgiving, and normally I'd be so excited to see them, they're lovely people, his mom makes this incredible sweet potato casserole, but the second he mentioned flying down there, I just completely shut down. I couldn't even talk about it. So yeah, it's really the whole experience now, from start to finish, just the whole idea of it is too much.
Have you been able to get on a plane at all since that flight, or have you been avoiding flying completely?

Oh, completely avoiding it. I haven't stepped foot in an airport since we landed back home from that honeymoon. It's actually becoming a bit of a problem, to be honest, because it takes so much extra effort to work around it. Like, I've been intentionally choosing these ridiculously long drives just to get out of it. A few months ago, my sister had a baby shower a couple of states over, and instead of taking a quick two-hour flight, which would have been so easy and honestly a lot cheaper, I literally drove fourteen hours straight. My back was absolutely killing me, and I had to stop at all these sketchy gas stations in the middle of the night, but I just couldn't bring myself to book the flight. 

And it's affecting my job, too. Being an administrator at the daycare, there are these early childhood education conferences and work trainings that I'm supposed to go to—really great networking events, you know, where they talk about new curriculum standards, state regulations, and all that important stuff—and I've just been turning them down flat out if they require getting on a plane. I always make up some excuse about being needed at the center to cover shifts, or having too much paperwork, but really it's just the flying. 

Even just *talking* about a potential trip is a whole ordeal. Like I mentioned with that Florida trip for Thanksgiving... if we absolutely have to sit down and discuss travel plans, or even just look at the logistics of going somewhere far away, I literally need my husband sitting right there next to me just to get through the conversation without completely backing out. He has to sit with me on the couch while we talk about it, otherwise I just panic and cancel the whole idea in my head. So, yeah, no planes. Not even close. I just go entirely out of my way to avoid it now.
When you think about flying or even talk about travel plans, do you notice symptoms like a racing heart, shortness of breath, or feeling like you're having a panic attack?

Oh, absolutely. Yes. It's incredibly physical, which is honestly one of the most frustrating parts about all of this. Like, if I'm just sitting at my desk at the center... I have this little office right off the main playroom... and if I'm sitting there on my laptop, just looking at flights for one of those conferences I mentioned, even just typing in the destination or seeing the flight options pop up on the screen, my chest just completely tightens up right away. It's like someone is pulling a tight band around my ribs. 

And I get this massive, overwhelming rush of panic. It's so intense that my immediate instinct is just... I have to get away from it right that second. I literally will just slam the laptop shut. Just close it and push it away from me across the desk, like it's dangerous or something. I just need to get away from the thought of it before it completely takes over. 

And the crazy thing is, it's not even just when I'm actively looking at tickets. We have outdoor playground time with the toddlers usually around 10:30 in the morning, and sometimes a plane will fly over. We're not super close to the airport, but close enough that you can hear them, especially the big commercial ones, and the kids will point up and yell about the airplane... and just hearing that low engine sound overhead triggers that exact same response. My chest seizes up, I get that same sudden rush of panic, and I just want to run back inside the building. It's this instant, immediate reaction, like my body is sounding an alarm, even though I'm perfectly safe on the ground just watching kids on the swings. It just hits me so fast, before I can even try to logic my way out of it.

Do you find yourself worrying about flying even when you’re not actively planning a trip or thinking about a specific flight, like having anxiety that it might come up or that you might be exposed to it unexpectedly?

You know, it's funny, because with how intense that panic is when it actually happens, you would probably think I'd be sitting around stressing about it all day long, but... honestly, no, not really. I don't just sit there and worry about it out of nowhere. 

My days are so incredibly packed, I just don't have the mental space for it. I mean, running the administrative side of a daycare center is just non-stop from the second I walk in at 7:00 AM until I lock the doors at 6:00 PM. We have seventy-five kids enrolled right now, and between managing the staff schedules, dealing with parents who are upset about the new late pickup fees—which we completely had to implement because people were just taking advantage and leaving our teachers waiting around—and making sure all our state compliance paperwork is perfectly in order... my brain is just entirely occupied with a million other things. 

So if I'm not actively looking at a flight on my computer, or my husband hasn't brought up a trip, or a plane isn't literally flying right over the playground while we're outside, I'm really not thinking about flying at all. It's not like this dark cloud hanging over my head every second of the day, where I'm constantly terrified that someone is going to suddenly force me to go to the airport. I don't have that dread just... hovering there in the background. 

When I go home, I'm cooking dinner, I'm watching my shows, I'm talking to my husband about his day at work, and I'm completely fine. I feel totally normal. It really only rears its ugly head when the topic is actually on the table, or like I said, if I hear one overhead. But just sitting around anticipating it or worrying that it might come up? No, I don't really do that. And thank goodness, honestly, because I think if I was worrying about airplanes 24/7 on top of everything else I have to manage at the center, I would probably just lose my mind completely.
Do you ever feel anxious about flying even when there’s no upcoming trip or discussion of travel?

I mean, I think I just said this, but no, not really. I don't just sit around feeling anxious about it for no reason. Like I was saying, my days are just so chaotic at the daycare. There's always a crisis, always a parent who forgot to pack a lunch or a teacher calling out sick at the absolute last minute, so I'm constantly putting out fires. I don't have the luxury of just sitting at my desk twiddling my thumbs and imagining being on an airplane. 

And even when I'm home, I'm just trying to decompress, you know? I'll put on a podcast or we'll watch whatever show we're currently binging—right now it's this baking competition, which is so relaxing—and I'm just focused on that. I'm not sitting on the couch, totally safe in my living room, having a panic attack about a hypothetical flight that isn't even happening. It's really just when it's right in front of me, like if I have to look at a travel website or if we're actively talking about going somewhere that would require a plane. If it's not happening in reality, or at least being planned in reality, it's just not on my radar at all. I have way too many actual, real-life things to worry about to invent things to stress over, you know?
